title: Reading Longer Words in Syllables
keyIdea: Every syllable has one vowel sound, so to read a long word, find the vowels and cut the word into parts. Two consonants in the middle: cut between them (nap-kin). One consonant in the middle: try an open cut first, where the first part ends in a vowel and the vowel says its name (ti-ger); if that is not a real word, try a closed cut with a short vowel (cab-in). A word ending in a consonant plus le keeps those three letters together (ta-ble). Read each part, then blend them into the word.
familyTip: When your child gets stuck on a long word in a book, cover part of it with your finger. Ask them to find the vowels, read the first part, then slide your finger along and read the next. Then say it fast. Try it on a cereal box or a sign: pic-nic, can-dle, ro-bot.

visual.caption: Count the vowel sounds. How many syllables? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: tap the vowel sounds, cut between two consonants, try open then closed, keep consonant-le together, and sort open and closed syllables.

kid: Long words are easier to read in parts. Each part is a syllable. Each syllable has one vowel sound. So find the vowels first: a, e, i, o and u.
Two vowels side by side often make one sound, like ai in rain or oa in boat. That counts as one vowel sound, so rain has one syllable.
Look between the vowels. Two consonants? Cut between them: nap-kin, rab-bit. One consonant? Try ti-ger first, where the i says its name. If it does not sound right, cut after it: cab-in.
A word that ends with a consonant and le keeps them together: ta-ble, can-dle. Now read each part and say them fast. You just read a long word!
adult: Ages 6 to 9. This is the decoding step after children can hear and clap syllables. Common Core RF.1.3d and RF.1.3e ask children to use the fact that every syllable has a vowel sound and to decode two-syllable words by breaking them into syllables; RF.2.3c and RF.3.3c extend this to long vowels and longer words. In England, Year 1 children read words of more than one syllable containing taught grapheme-phoneme correspondences, and Years 2 to 4 build fluency with longer words.

The patterns are named by the letters between the vowels. VC/CV: two consonants, split between them (bas-ket), giving closed syllables with short vowels. V/CV: one consonant, first try an open syllable that ends in the vowel, which is long (mu-sic). VC/V: if the open try is not a real word, move the cut so the first syllable is closed and short (lem-on). Consonant-le: the consonant before le joins it (pud-dle). Vowel teams such as ai, ea and oa are never split.

These are reading strategies, not spelling laws or dictionary hyphenation. Their job is to give a child a pronounceable try that they then check against words they know. That is why the V/CV rule says try open first and flex if it does not make sense.

Common mistakes: counting vowel letters instead of vowel sounds (rain is one syllable), leaving a part with no vowel (p-ilot), always cutting after the first vowel (ca-bin read as cay-bin), and cutting consonant-le the wrong way (tab-le). In the lab your child marks vowel sounds, cuts words at the gaps, picks open or closed, keeps le with its consonant and sorts first syllables.

practice.prompt: Where does napkin split into syllables?
practice.hint: Find the two consonants in the middle, p and k. Cut between them.
practice.explain: Nap-kin: two consonants sit between the vowels, so the cut goes between them. Both parts are closed, so the a and i are short.

practice.prompt: Leo has {n} word cards. One says rain. He says rain has 2 syllables, because it has a and i. Is he right?
choices: No, ai is one vowel sound, so 1 syllable
practice.hint: Say rain. Is the ai one sound or two?
practice.explain: The a and i in rain are a vowel team. They make one sound, so rain has one syllable. Count sounds, not letters.

practice.prompt: Which way does tiger make a real word?
choices: ti | ger, with a long i
tig | er, with a short i
practice.hint: Try the open cut first: the first part ends in a vowel, so the vowel says its name.
practice.explain: Ti-ger: ti is an open syllable, so the i says its name. Tig-er does not sound like a word, and t has no vowel.

practice.prompt: Mia reads {n} words with le at the end. Where does candle split?
practice.hint: The le takes the consonant just before it: dle.
practice.explain: Can-dle: consonant-le stays together as dle, and the n goes with can. Cand-le splits the consonant from its le.

practice.prompt: Cabin has one consonant between the vowels. Ca-bin sounds like cay-bin. What should you try next?
choices: Cut after the b: cab-in, with a short a
practice.hint: If the open try is not a real word, move the cut one letter on.
practice.explain: Cay-bin is not a word, so flex: cab-in makes the first syllable closed, with a short a. Now it sounds right. C-abin leaves a part with no vowel.

pool.hint: Two consonants in the middle: cut between them.
pool.explain: Rab-bit splits between the two b letters. Each part has one vowel sound, and both vowels are short.

pool.prompt: How many syllables does teapot have?
pool.hint: Find the vowel sounds. Is ea one sound?
pool.explain: Tea-pot has two vowel sounds, ea and o, so two syllables. The ea team counts once, so it is not three.

pool.hint: One consonant in the middle. Try open first.
pool.explain: Ro-bot: try open first, and ro with a long o makes a real word. Rob-ot does not, and r has no vowel.

pool.hint: Try open first: lee-mon. Is that a real word? If not, flex.
pool.explain: Lee-mon is not a word, so move the cut: lem-on, with a short e. That is the word you know.

pool.hint: Consonant-le stays together. Find the letter just before le.
pool.explain: Pud-dle: the d before le joins it to make dle, and pud keeps the other d. Pudd-le breaks up the consonant-le.

pool.prompt: Ava splits {n} words. She cuts pilot as p | ilot. What is wrong?
choices: The part p has no vowel
pool.hint: Look at each part. Does each one have a vowel sound?
pool.explain: Every syllable needs a vowel sound, and p has none. The right cut is pi-lot, an open first syllable with a long i.

pool.prompt: Ben has {n} words to sort. Is the first part of paper open or closed?
choices: Open: pa ends in a vowel, so the a is long
Closed: pa ends in a consonant
Closed: paper has two p letters
pool.hint: Look at the last letter of pa.
pool.explain: Pa ends in the vowel a, so it is open and the a says its name. Closed syllables end in a consonant, like nap in napkin.

pool.hint: Find the two consonants between the vowels a and e.
pool.explain: The consonants s and k sit between the vowels, so cut between them: bas-ket. Both parts are closed, with short vowels.

pool.prompt: How many syllables does sunset have?
pool.hint: Count the vowel sounds, u and e.
pool.explain: Sun-set has two vowel sounds, so two syllables. Six is how many letters it has, which is a different count.
